A1-A2.headline: The Historic Shooting That Started World War One

pages.text: On June 28, 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie were shot in Sarajevo. This tragic event changed world history forever. Two people lost their lives while riding through the city in an open car.
pages.caption: Assassination illustrated in La Domenica del Corriere

evidence.articleCaption: Assassination illustrated in the Italian newspaper La Domenica del Corriere, 12 July 1914 by Achille Beltrame

pages.text: The man who shot them was Gavrilo Princip. He was a young student from a group called Young Bosnia. The group wanted to free their homeland from Austro-Hungarian rule.
pages.caption: Gavrilo Princip outside the courthouse

pages.text:
Most of the six attackers were very young men under twenty years old. Only one man in the group was older. In October 1914, a court in Sarajevo put twenty-five people on trial for the attack.

Because of his young age, Gavrilo Princip could not be put to death. Instead, the judge gave him twenty years in prison. Four other young attackers also went to prison, while five older men were sentenced to death.

This shocking attack started a major political crisis across Europe. Leaders in Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia for helping the young attackers. Soon after, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia.

Other countries in Europe quickly joined the fight to support their friends. This terrible conflict grew into a huge war that became known as the First World War.

B1-B2.headline: The Sarajevo Assassination That Triggered World War One

pages.text: On June 28, 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie were assassinated in Sarajevo. Their fatal shooting by a nationalist revolutionary group dramatically altered the course of European history.
pages.caption: Assassination illustrated in La Domenica del Corriere

evidence.articleCaption: Assassination illustrated in the Italian newspaper La Domenica del Corriere, 12 July 1914 by Achille Beltrame

pages.text: The principal attacker, Gavrilo Princip, belonged to Young Bosnia, a movement dedicated to ending Austro-Hungarian rule and establishing a united South Slav state. The conspirators received critical weapons and tactical training from the Black Hand.
pages.caption: Gavrilo Princip outside the courthouse

pages.text:
Following the coordinated attacks, Austro-Hungarian authorities arrested twenty-five individuals, including the assassins and local agents who had helped them. Most were charged with high treason.

The subsequent trials in Sarajevo in October 1914 led to multiple prison sentences and five executions. Because Princip was under twenty years old, he was legally spared the death penalty and received a twenty-year jail term.

Before the visit, Serbian diplomats reportedly gave general warnings about possible danger in Bosnia, though Austro-Hungarian officials dismissed them and Serbia later denied knowing about the plot.

After the murders, the July Crisis swept across European capitals. Austria-Hungary swiftly declared war on Serbia, setting off a devastating chain reaction that ignited the First World War.

C1-C2.headline: The Geopolitical Repercussions of the Sarajevo Assassination

pages.text: On 28 June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir presumptive to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie were assassinated in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip. This pivotal event ruptured European stability and catalyzed the July Crisis.
pages.caption: Assassination illustrated in La Domenica del Corriere

evidence.articleCaption: Assassination illustrated in the Italian newspaper La Domenica del Corriere, 12 July 1914 by Achille Beltrame

pages.text:
Princip acted as part of Young Bosnia, a revolutionary network seeking to liberate Bosnia and Herzegovina from Austro-Hungarian administration and establish a unified South Slav state.

Clandestine support, including bombs, pistols, and tactical training, was funneled through the Black Hand, a Serbian secret nationalist organization involving senior military intelligence figures.

Subsequent judicial proceedings in Sarajevo in October 1914 indicted twenty-five individuals, including the assassins and local agents charged with conspiracy to commit high treason.

Because Princip was under twenty years old, legal age exceptions spared him from capital punishment, resulting instead in a twenty-year prison sentence, while five older accomplices were sentenced to hang.

Despite vague preliminary warnings transmitted by Serbian diplomats, Austro-Hungarian ministers largely dismissed the risks; historical accounts remain nuanced, as Belgrade subsequently denied prior knowledge of the plot.

The ensuing declarations of hostilities manifested the catastrophic vulnerability of pre-war international alliances, plunging Europe into the First World War.
